Notice that the logarithms share the same base. 

First, we apply the power rule to the first term to make the coefficient in front of each logarithm the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(4x)-2{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2})=1 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(4x)-{log}_{2}⁡({({x}^{2})}^{2})=1 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(4x)-{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{4}) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we combine the logarithms using the quotient rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(\frac{4x}{{x}^{4}}) & =1 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(\frac{4}{{x}^{3}}) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing this equation in its equivalent exponential form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{{x}^{3}} & ={2}^{1} \\ \frac{4}{{x}^{3}} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve this rational equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{{x}^{3}} & =2 \\ {x}^{3}\cdot \frac{4}{{x}^{3}} & ={x}^{3}\cdot 2 \\ \cancel{{x}^{3}}\cdot \frac{4}{\cancel{{x}^{3}}} & =2{x}^{3} \\ 2{x}^{3} & =4 \\ {x}^{3} & =2 \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now check for an extraneous solution by substituting back into the original equation: 

Substituting $x=\sqrt[3]{2}$ back into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(4(\sqrt[3]{2}))-2{log}_{2}⁡((\sqrt[3]{2})^{2}) & \overset{?}{=}1 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(4(\sqrt[3]{2}))-{log}_{2}⁡{((\sqrt[3]{2})^{2})}^{2} & \overset{?}{=}1 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(4(\sqrt[3]{2}))-{log}_{2}⁡((\sqrt[3]{2})^{4}) & \overset{?}{=}1 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(4(\sqrt[3]{2}))-{log}_{2}⁡(2(\sqrt[3]{2})) & \overset{?}{=}1 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(\frac{4\sqrt[3]{2}}{2\sqrt[3]{2}}) & \overset{?}{=}1 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(\frac{4\cancel{\sqrt[3]{2}}}{2\cancel{\sqrt[3]{2}}}) & \overset{?}{=}1 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(\frac{4}{2}) & \overset{?}{=}1 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(2) & \overset{?}{=}1 \\ 1 & =1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=\sqrt[3]{2}$ is a valid solution.
